title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: the problem preceding Problem V, whose statement is not on the supplied pages. Euler seeks a space curve x,y,z extremizing an integral that depends on v = √(x²+y²+z²) and the arc element. On the previous page he showed the extremal lies in a plane z = ny + ax. With p = dy/dx and y = ux he reduced the remaining Euler–Lagrange relation y dx − x dy = v² dp/s² to a separated equation with identical members:
−du/(1+u²+(nu+a)²) = dp/(1+p²+(np+a)²).

On this page:
(1) He writes 1+p²+(np+a)² = (1+n²)(p²+2αp+β), with α = an/(1+n²) and β = (1+a²)/(1+n²). He substitutes t = p+α and integrates: ∫dp/(…) = [1/((1+n²)√(β−α²))]·arctan((p+α)/√(β−α²)). The u-member is the same with a minus sign.
(2) Since the coefficients agree, the integral is arctan(U) + arctan(P) = C, where P = (p+α)/k, U = (u+α)/k and k = √(β−α²). Taking the tangent of the sum gives k(p+u+2α)/(β−2α²−α(p+u)−pu) = const. This is the algebraic relation pu + α(p+u) + 2α² − β = C(p+u+2α). After renaming the constant it becomes pu − β = f(p+u+2α), i.e. (1+n²)pu − a² − 1 = f((1+n²)(p+u)+2an).
(3) This is still a first-order ODE, since u = y/x and p = y′. From y = ux one gets dx/x = du/(p−u). The relation is linear in p, so p is a rational function of u and the equation separates.
(4) The next page carries out the quadrature algebraically and finds that both projections of the curve are central conics centred at the origin.

Geometric meaning, not stated by Euler: in the plane of the curve, the separated equation says (polar angle of the radius vector) + (inclination of the tangent) = const. Curves with this property are rectangular hyperbolas centred at O. They are the extremals of ∫ r ds (the metric |z||dz|, straightened by w = z²). The oblique projection of such a hyperbola onto the xy-plane is the general central conic Euler finds.
errors: No error on this page. The arctangent integrals and the tangent-addition step check out. The sign and shift of the constant (C → f = C − α, up to sign) is legitimately absorbed into the arbitrary constant.

On the next page, x²(g+2af+2fu−u²) = const with u = y/x gives gx² + 2afx² + 2fxy − y² = const. The printed −2fxy appears to be a sign slip (or a transcription error). The constant is written g again, which reuses the letter. Neither affects the conclusion that the curve is a conic.
On the next page the letters a and g silently stand for α and β of this page.

ideas.what: Integrating dp/(quadratic) by completing the square to an arctangent
Converting a sum of two arctangents equal to a constant into an algebraic relation via the tangent addition formula, i.e. an algebraic first integral
ideas.modern_name: Addition theorem for arctan (the elementary prototype of Euler's addition-theorem method)
ideas.where_published: Used throughout Euler's work on separated equations dx/√X = dy/√Y

ideas.what: Reduction of the homogeneous-type relation F(p,y/x) = 0 via y = ux to a separable equation dx/x = du/(p−u)
Extremals of the central-type functional are planar curves whose projections are central conics (in-plane: rectangular hyperbolas centred at the origin)
ideas.modern_name: Geodesics of the conformal metric r|dz|, i.e. images of lines under z ↦ z²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Planar case known in 18th-c. variational literature; the conformal-map interpretation is 19th c.
ideas.where_published: Planar analogue probably in Methodus inveniendi (1744); unsure

missed.claim: The separated equation is the statement 'polar angle + tangent inclination = const' in the plane of the curve. This characterizes rectangular hyperbolas centred at O, the straight lines in the coordinate w = z². Euler only reports 'some conic section' for the projections and does not identify the in-plane curve as a rectangular hyperbola. It is a small, well-known fact, not a genuine gap in the literature.
missed.quote: sive summa horum duorum arcuum aequatur quantitati constanti
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor. It illustrates an early instance of an angle-sum invariant that later becomes the conformal-map (z²) description of these extremals. This is not new to specialists.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine integration and arctan-addition algebra on a standard variational problem whose answer (planar central conics) is classical. It is correct, with nothing apparently absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Previous page: '1 + aa + 2anp (nn + 1)pp' should read '1 + aa + 2anp + (nn+1)pp'.
This page matches the image. The constant on the right of the tangent equation is printed 'C' and is a different constant from the C in the arctan equation, as in the original.
